newsitem.title: FRANCE: France ready to send troops for Mideast peace.
newsitem.headline: France ready to send troops for Mideast peace.

text.p: France said on Thursday it was ready to send troops to the Middle East to guarantee a possible peace accord on Israel's borders with Lebanon and Syria if the United States and other Western powers also took part.

"France is ready to participate in a global Lebanese-Syrian accord with Israel, but with other countries too including the United States and France as guarantors, as witnesses so that the principle of land for peace...can be enacted with Syria and Lebanon as it was with other Middle East countries," Defence Minister Charles Millon said.

Interviewed by Europe 1 radio while on an official visit to Israel, Millon did not answer directly when asked if he meant Paris was prepared to put soldiers on the ground in the Golan Heights and the explosive Israel-Lebanon border area.
But one of his senior advisers told reporters in Paris: "Yes, we are ready to participate in such an operation but in a multinational framework and with the accord of all the parties concerned."
The adviser said the peace force would be separate from the existing United Nations force, UNIFIL, on the Israel-Lebanon border, which has long been criticised as ineffective.
France, keen to stay on good terms with both sides in the Arab-Israeli conflict, had been campaigning for the European Union to have a bigger role in Middle East peacemaking.
The force could exist only if it were stationed on both the Israel-Syria and Israel-Lebanon borders, the aide said.
Millon's visit was a sign of warming defence relations with Israel. Franco-Israeli ties were icy after Paris slapped an arms embargo on the Jewish state following the 1967 Middle East war.
Links were revived four years ago by then defence minister Francois Leotard.
"Even if there have been high and low points in our relations, all friendships are made of highs and lows. Today France reaffirms its friendship with Israel and vice-versa," Millon said.
But he said France was cautious on defence and aerospace cooperation with Israel as with other countries of the region.
"We want to take part in a peace process, it is out of the question that we take part in an arms race," the minister said.

Millon's visit is one of several ministerial visits recently announced by Prime Minister Alain Juppe, seeking to mend fences with the Jewish community before a 1998 general election after President Jacques Chirac's shouting match with Israeli security men in Jerusalem last October.
